en: The young champion, the noble lord’s son,
Was seized fast by bloodlust.
“If fate arrives, I will die;
If I do not die, I will see the face
Of my leopard, Sultan Khan and uncle!
If the fiercest of the bastard Chinese
Falls into my hands,
I will make a spectacle of him!”
The gray wolf pondered and said this,
Put on Akolpok,
And gathered himself like a white tiger—
The splendid hero, the lion’s son.
From valiant Manas, the gray wolf,
The gray kise remained as a gift;
To pursue the blood-price from Beijing,
He girded it tight around his sturdy waist.
Gathering himself like a lion,
He donned the bulletproof coat,
Prayed to his Allah,
And the valiant man’s son prepared
To make a lone raid upon Beijing.
He put on the coat Akolpok
And slung Akkelte across his back.
His face turned wrathful,
Zulpukor, left by Manas,
Your young champion girded on.
The helmet of blue iron
Had been fashioned by poor Kanykei;
Your valiant mother Kanykei
Had given it as a gift, weeping bitterly.
Valiant Lady Kanykei
So no axe would pierce his head,
She had dedicated it as a gift.
The splendid hero, the valiant man’s son,
Lifted the helmet of blue iron
And placed it upon his head.
The poor father’s son
Crossed its fastening cords
And tied them beneath his throat.
The armor for his ribs,
Chosen and given by Kanykei—
He fastened the bulletproof iron
Over his entire body,
Every part of his broad frame
He plated over with blue iron.
He armed himself in fury,
Readying all his weapons of war,
May your gray wolf’s road be blessed,
His waist-girdle fastened firm;
Your young champion had set out
To bring Kongurbai down.
To die, if death should reach him,
Or, if his strength sufficed, the countless foe
To raid them all and return—
Eagerly braced for the deed,
The valiant prince then
Swayed as though struck by a blow.
His thoughts, it seemed, were divided;
He loomed like Mount Opol.
The young man turned and spoke,
To his uncle, valiant Bakai,
Words of a dread, irrevocable fate:
“Uncle Bakai, leopard,
Thinking, ‘My son has ridden out on patrol,’
Do not grieve, my holy sage!
I am going to meet
The decree the Creator has written!
If death reaches me in Beijing,
I am going there to die!
Gripping my spear, I shall break their ranks;
If death reaches me, I shall fall to a bullet!
On the path of my poor father
I shall die as a sacrifice.
Kongurbai, khan of the Chinese,
I shall meet in a fierce contest
And return after wreaking slaughter!
Kongurbai is the one I shall fight;
Upon that swine, the khan of the Kechil,
I shall lay bitter grief!
If my lion father supports me,
The lion of the lower Black Chinese
I shall split in two;
With that slave, the khan of the Kechil,
I shall meet and then return!
Do not grieve, my uncle Bakai;
Go on living without sorrow,
And for your cherished young son
Mourn for six days!
If I have not returned in six days,
I shall have been left afoot in the rear—
Take your two sons away,
And sweep onward to your mirror-bright city;
Say, ‘My beloved son has died,’
And give up all hope of me!
I am going to open up
One whole face of the open steppe,
And with clamorous cries, their countless herds
I am going to scatter!
I go to confront
Great Kongurbai the Kalmak;
If death arrives and my days are done,
I am going to meet it.
My uncle Bakai, brave gray wolf,
Against the mighty khan of the Kechil,
How could I remain without going?
How could I fail to raise
Red slaughter and roaring battle cries?
Kongurbai is the one I shall face;
If my strength comes, the Chinese
I shall offer up as sacrifice.
With the infidel whose surge is mountain-high
I shall grapple in combat!
Against the heroic khan of Kalday
I shall unleash havoc;
With that thundering dog
I shall fight to the finish.
If fate reaches me, I shall die;
If my heroic father supports me,
Kongurbai’s countless horses
I shall raid and drive off, every one!
I shall bring them mighty grief;
From Kürpüldök and Keng-Shor
I shall seize the horses without delay!
Turn Kokcholok’s head, uncle,
And wait, thinking, ‘When will my gray wolf return?’
Yearn for your son as you wait, uncle!”
The bulletproof Akolpok—
Your formidable son now put it on.
There was no hole in Akolpok;
For the young son of the bloodletter,
No foe who challenged him would prosper!
The armor left by his father Manas
He pulled on over the rest.
Its buttons numbered nine;
Across his very breast
He matched up all the buttons.
Its fastening cords numbered nine;
He secured every cord.
The gray kise that fell from heaven
Your valiant hero now buckled at his waist.
His face turned wrathful,
And the lion-warrior’s Zulpukor
He fastened at his left side.
When he slung on that fine thing,
It was a mirror upon his shoulder,
And when he entered battle with the foe,
A shield for his entrusted life.
Almabash, the keenest iron,
Made no distinction between far and near;
When your lion wielded it in war,
It would not dull for sixty days.
Look closely: this was the treasure,
The keen blade inherited
From Manas, the gray wolf of old.
Your noble hero’s Akkelte
He now slung upon his shoulder.
Brimming over with fierce spirit,
He covered the matchless stallion
Carefully with its cloth,
So that no stray bullet would strike it.
Wary of the Chinese side,
Upon the great dapple-gray
He fitted the white saddle.
Into the gold-soled stirrups
Your young champion, the noble lord’s son,
Stretched tall and mounted his horse.
He buckled on the scabbardless sword,
And saying, “Mighty Allah, grant me a road!”
Turned toward the khan.
Lamenting in many ways,
Your uncle Bakai, the lion-warrior,
Was left standing gaunt upon the ridge.
The splendid warrior, the valiant man’s son,
Rode proudly toward Beijing.
His eyes were broad as the reaches of a lake,
As though they could devour anyone he saw.
The great Buurul,
That ill-fated, hapless steed,
He made buck and strain;
The peerless Buurul
The leopard-prince made heave and plunge
As though its master had died.
Its tail stood apart, its mane was low;
The poor hero’s Buurul
Had a forelock that did not hang long,
But seemed tied to fit its eyes;
Everyone who saw it
Would burn with longing,
Wishing, “If only that horse were mine!”
When one looked from behind,
The breadth of its croup
Was like a separate open plain;
The size of its hoof
Was like an upturned basin.
Its spreading haunches were like a ravine;
The matchless Arbuurul—
No wind could match it at a trot,
No beast could match its pace.
It flung its forelock to the sky,
And drove its hooves into the earth;
When it bounded, its great stride
Hurled a road’s length, broad as a house,
Stepping on with its rolling gait,
Loping with a bounding gait,
Gathering itself in rolling surges,
Sweeping on as though pitching headlong,
He flew along upon Buurul.
Delighting in its pace,
Behind him the dust
Trailed like a mountain.
His sword buckled on in eagerness,
Your gray wolf, blessed by Kydyr,
Rounded Kaspan’s Kara-Too,
Crossing rugged mountain country,
And when he came to certain places,
Crossing shimmering desert wastes.
The noble hero journeyed without stint;
The horse covered a vast distance.
How could your valiant hero spare himself?
He drew near the herds,
Your young champion, the noble lord’s son,
Approaching Kyr-Kaying.
When he reached Kyr-Kaying,
There was a gaping gorge;
When he looked below,
There stretched a boundless forest,
And when he looked this way,
There was a black ridge curved like a sickle.
“This must be the place
My formidable uncle Bakai foretold.
Let me take the measure of the land,
And learn how many warriors there are;
Let me reconnoiter their route,
And count how many heroes they have.
Let me count them one by one
And learn the worth of their courage;
Let me set all the accursed man’s horses moving
And raid every one of them;
Let me learn the number
Of the horses doomed to be left masterless!”
So saying, Semetey then
Made his way up that mountain,
To its jutting black ridge,
To the place his formidable uncle Bakai
Had marked out for him.
When he reached the ridge,
Do not ask how the valiant hero fared:
In the hollow of Kara-Kyr,
Along the Kara-Archa,
Your bloodletter now dismounted.
The splendid hero, son of Manas,
Was ready to draw the line,
To raid the khan’s horses
And make a spectacle of the deed.
